items.prose: Two threads run code that uses these four names.
items.question: Which are shared by both threads? Select all that apply.

options.text: A local `int n` captured by reference in a lambda both threads run

options.why: `thread_local` gives each thread its own copy.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which exist once, or are reached through a reference?

explain.text: A `static` and a file-scope mutex exist once per process. A reference capture shares the local it names. `thread_local` is the one name here that each thread owns.

items.prose: Creating a thread costs 15 µs. A handler makes a new thread for every message, at 100,000 messages a second.
items.question: How many cores does creating the threads use?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the cost by the rate.

byKey.fifteen: You slipped a power of ten: $15 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^5 = 1.5$.
byKey.tenth: You slipped a power of ten the other way.

explain.text: $15 \times 10^{-6}$ s $\times 100{,}000 = 1.5$ s of work every second. That is one and a half cores spent only on starting threads. A pool of threads made once avoids it.

items.prose: Two lanes each run load `x`, add 1, store `x`, from `x = 0`.
items.question: How many of the 20 interleavings end with `x` at 2?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. When does neither update get lost?

byKey.most: 18 is the count that ends at 1.
byKey.half: The orders are not split evenly.

explain.text: `x` ends at 2 only when one lane runs whole before the other loads. That is a, a, a, b, b, b or the reverse. The other 18 lose an update.

items.prose: Three lanes each run load `x`, add 1, store `x`, from `x = 0`.
items.question: Which finals can happen? Select all that apply.

options.why: Every store writes a load plus 1.
Three adds of 1 reach 3 at most.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the least and the most a store can write.

explain.text: All three loads can read 0, giving 1; one lost update gives 2, and serial orders give 3. Of the 1,680 interleavings, 1,404 end at 1, 270 at 2 and 6 at 3. Nothing gives 0 or 4.

items.prose: Three threads take locks in the orders AB, BC and CA, each holding the first while taking the second.
items.question: Can they deadlock, and what is the fix?

options.text: Yes: A to B to C to A is a cycle; reverse one thread's order
No: no two threads take the same pair
options.why: A cycle can run through three threads; follow the edges.

options.text: Yes, and nothing short of one global lock fixes it
options.why: Reversing one thread's order breaks the cycle.

options.text: Only if two of them start at once
options.why: All three must hold their first lock, but that can happen.

feedback.correct: Yes. Reverse one thread, so every thread takes A, B, C in order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Draw an edge for each thread.

explain.text: The edges A to B, B to C and C to A form a ring of waits. If the third thread takes A then C, every edge follows A, B, C. Of the 168 schedules of the ring, 6 deadlock; after the fix none do.

items.prose: T1 takes lock A then B; T2 takes B then A. A lane cannot step while the lock it wants is held.
items.question: How many of the 6 legal schedules deadlock?

widget.accept: 2: each lane takes its first lock, in either order.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. When do both lanes hold one lock each?

byKey.one: Either lane can take its first lock first: two ways.

explain.text: Both lanes stick only when both first locks are taken before either second lock. That happens in two orders. The other four schedules finish.

items.prose: Thread A sets `x = 1`, then reads `y` into `r1`. Thread B sets `y = 1`, then reads `x` into `r2`. Both start at 0. Suppose the four steps run one at a time, in some order, with no store buffer.
items.question: Which pairs (r1, r2) can occur? Select all that apply.

options.why: Each lane stores before it loads, so the later load always sees a 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Can both loads come before both stores?

byKey.p00: Each lane's store comes first in its own lane, so the last load sees a 1.

explain.text: Whichever load runs last, the other lane's store has run before it. So at least one register is 1. Real cores with `relaxed` atomics can still give (0, 0), because a store can wait in a buffer.

items.prose: A consumer checks whether the queue is empty, then waits for a notify. A producer pushes, then notifies. Sometimes the consumer sleeps forever with an item queued.
items.question: Why?

options.text: The check and the wait were not under one lock, and the notify came in between

options.why: A spurious wakeup ends a wait early; it never makes one endless.
A full queue blocks the producer, not the consumer.
There is only one consumer, so either wakes it, if it is waiting.

feedback.correct: The notify fell between the check and the wait.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. When does a notify wake nobody?

explain.text: A notify wakes only threads already waiting. If the push and notify land after the check but before the wait, the consumer sleeps through them. Holding the mutex across the check and the wait closes that gap.

items.prose: Two counters sit on one 64-byte cache line. Each is incremented by its own thread. An add costs 60 ns when the line moves between cores. It costs 1 ns when the line stays in one core's L1.
items.question: Moving one counter to its own line makes each add how many times faster?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two costs per add.

byKey.two: There are two counters, but the cost is per add.
byKey.sixtyfour: 64 is the line size in bytes, not a cost.

explain.text: The threads never share a counter, but they share a line, so the line moves on every add. This is false sharing. Padding each counter to its own 64-byte line drops the add from 60 ns to 1 ns.
